# Token or No Token

Source: https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-12 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A token should reduce coordination cost or create ownership; if it does neither, do not issue one. If you do, the money you raise decides your go-to-market, and float, release schedules, stablecoin runway and liquidity depth matter more than headline FDV. The 2026 US and EU position makes what you promise in public part of the legal analysis, so legal belongs inside GTM.

A token should reduce coordination cost or create ownership. If it does neither, do not issue one, and if you do, the type of money you raise decides your go-to-market before you write a line of it. Circulating float, the release schedule, stablecoin runway and liquidity depth say more than headline FDV. And in 2026 the US and EU both tie the legal treatment of a token to what the team says about it, so legal review is part of GTM, not a box ticked before it.

*This is not investment or legal advice. Token structures are fact-specific; get your own counsel.*

## What a token is actually for

Strip away the narrative and a token does one of two jobs. It coordinates people who do not trust each other, or it gives them ownership they cannot get another way.

Everything else is a worse version of something cheaper. Settlement can run on stablecoins. Loyalty can run on points. Access control can run on a database with a login page.

So the first question is not "what will our token do". It is "what breaks if we do not have one". If nothing breaks, you have your answer for now. You are not closing the door. You are refusing to open it before the room is built.

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) argued for raising on proof. In crypto, the token is where narrative hides best. Treat it with the same discipline, and write the answer down as a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with a reason and an owner, reviewed by someone outside the founding team.

## Three kinds of money and what each wants

The money you take is a GTM commitment. Each source wants something different from how you go to market.

| Source | What they are buying | What it pulls your GTM towards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equity only | A business that compounds | Revenue, retention, a product that sells without a token |
| Equity plus token warrant | A business and a launch event | A credible launch date, exchange relationships, a liquid market |
| Ecosystem or foundation money | Activity on their chain | Building where they live: their users, their events, their co-marketing |

None of these is wrong. All of them are binding. Ecosystem money in particular is often read as cheap grant capital. It is not. It is a distribution deal, and chain choice is the term that matters most. If you build on a chain because the grant was there, you have chosen your first hundred users without meeting them. Make sure they are the users you want.

## Float, release schedules and runway beat FDV

Headline FDV is the number people quote at dinner. It tells you almost nothing about the next eighteen months, and the evidence suggests a high one is a liability. Keyrock's review of 62 airdrop launches found higher launch FDV correlated with a greater likelihood of a significant price drop. One token in its sample launched at a $13 billion FDV with an estimated $6 million of liquidity, and fell 83%.

Three numbers tell you more. Circulating float at launch, because thin float means price is a story, not a market. The release schedule, because every cliff is a sell event you have to plan communications around. Treasury runway in stablecoins, because a treasury denominated in your own token is runway you cannot spend in a drawdown.

US regulators now ask for the same numbers. The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published in August 2026, would require principles-based disclosure that, in the Congressional Research Service's summary, covers token economics: supply, pricing, lockups, release schedules and mechanisms for creating or destroying the asset. A team that already runs its GTM calendar off the release calendar has most of that section written.

Build the GTM calendar around the release calendar, not the other way round. If a large release lands the same month as your biggest product launch, one of them moves.

## Legal does not end at launch

The specifics belong with counsel. The general point is that legal clarity is a fact pattern, not a one-time stamp, and the 2026 position makes that more literal, not less.

| Jurisdiction | Current position, November 2026 | What it means for GTM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US, SEC and CFTC | Joint interpretation of 17 March 2026 sets five categories: digital commodities, collectibles, tools and payment stablecoins outside securities law; tokenised securities inside it. A non-security token can still be sold as part of an investment contract, which can end when promised efforts are completed or abandoned | What the team promises, when, and through which medium feeds the analysis. Chairman Atkins said promises that create reliance "must be explicit and unambiguous" |
| US, SEC proposal | Regulation Crypto Assets, proposed 18 August 2026: a $5 million four-year startup exemption, a fundraising exemption of up to $75 million in 12 months, and a safe harbor once promised efforts are complete. Comments closed 20 October 2026; not final | Plan for principles-based disclosure and antifraud liability whatever exemption you use |
| US, Congress | The CLARITY Act passed the House 294 to 134 in July 2025 but failed Senate cloture 49 to 50 on 15 September 2026; passage this Congress is widely seen as unlikely. The GENIUS Act of 2025 covers payment stablecoins | Agency rules can be reversed; build for uncertainty |
| EU, MiCA | White papers "shall not contain any assertions as regards the future value" of the token, must state it may lose value in part or in full, and marketing must be consistent with the white paper. The transitional period for service providers ended 1 July 2026 | Every public claim has to match a filed document; exchange and custody partners must be authorised |

The common thread is that a marketing claim your team makes in month nine can matter as much as the structure you set in month one. That makes legal part of GTM. Your claims register from [one truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) needs a legal reviewer with sign-off, not a courtesy copy. Our piece on [raising in a regulated category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/) covers how that changes the fundraising conversation.

> Legal clarity is a fact pattern, not a stamp. What you say in public in month nine is part of it.

## Liquidity depth is a product requirement

Founders treat liquidity as a market-maker problem. It is a product problem. If a user cannot enter or exit at reasonable size without moving the price, the token does not work as a coordination tool. It works as a trap. Users notice, and your most active users notice first.

Set a minimum liquidity depth as a product requirement, in writing, before launch. Fund it, or do not launch. This is the same logic as not shipping a checkout page that fails above a certain basket size.

## The readiness gate

Before any token launch, we ask teams to score themselves against a gate. Not a pass-fail test: a practice that forces the honest conversation before the calendar does.

| Dimension | Evidence that earns a high score |
| --- | --- |
| Retention without incentives | Cohorts returning with rewards switched off |
| Token necessity | A written answer to "what breaks without it", reviewed externally |
| Legal clarity | Counsel's analysis in each launch market, and a claims register with sign-off |
| Security review | Named, scoped and dated audits; unaudited components listed |
| Treasury runway | Months of runway in stablecoins |
| Distribution in place | Channels that deliver users without the token |
| Liquidity depth | A funded minimum depth |
| Comms readiness | Release calendar and launch calendar reconciled |
| Incident response | A named owner and a rehearsed plan |

Incident response is on the list because something will go wrong in the first week. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025, with one exchange compromise accounting for $1.5 billion. Score each dimension, write one sentence of evidence beside each score, and where the evidence is thin, the score is low, whatever the team feels. The thresholds are yours to set. The point is to make the decision visible, so a weak dimension gets fixed or gets owned. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) shows where that record lives.

Gateway card

### Before you issue a token

- Written answer to "what breaks without a token", reviewed by someone outside the founding team
- Funding source chosen with its GTM pull named, including chain choice as distribution
- Release calendar laid over the GTM calendar, with conflicts resolved
- Treasury runway stated in stablecoins, not in your own token
- Minimum liquidity depth written down as a product requirement and funded
- Counsel's view for each launch market, and a claims register with legal sign-off
- Readiness gate scored with evidence per dimension, and an incident response owner named

## lowob takeaways

- **Ask what breaks.** If nothing breaks without a token, do not issue one for now.
- **Money is a GTM choice.** Ecosystem money is a distribution deal, and chain choice is its main term.
- **Float, releases and runway.** They say more than FDV, and US disclosure proposals ask for them too.
- **Legal is part of GTM.** In the US and EU, what you say in public shapes how the token is treated.

## Common questions

### Does my crypto startup need a token?

Only if it reduces coordination cost between people who do not trust each other or creates ownership they cannot get another way. If nothing breaks without one, you have your answer for now.

### Is FDV a good metric for a token launch?

No. Keyrock found higher launch FDVs correlated with steeper price falls. Circulating float at launch, the release schedule and treasury runway in stablecoins tell you more about the next eighteen months.

### Are tokens securities in the US in 2026?

Under the SEC and CFTC interpretation of March 2026, many native network tokens, collectibles, tools and payment stablecoins are outside securities law, but a token sold with promises of managerial effort can be part of an investment contract. It is fact-specific; get counsel.

### What does MiCA require before a token launch in the EU?

For offers needing one, a white paper with no assertions on future value and a statement that the token may lose value, marketing consistent with it and not issued before it, and authorised service providers since the transitional period ended on 1 July 2026.

## Next move

Set a minimum liquidity depth as a product requirement, in writing, before launch. Fund it, or do not launch. Then lay the release calendar over the launch calendar and move whichever event collides.
